title: How Light Travels
subtitle: Straight lines, mirrors and lenses, and why the sky is a colour at all.

sections.title: Why do you have a shadow?
sections.body:
Stand in the sun and look at the ground. You have a shadow. Hold your hand in front of a torch and your hand has a shadow on the wall. Have you ever wondered why? Let’s find out together, step by step.

The reason is the single most important fact about light in everyday life: light travels in straight lines. Your body blocks the straight path from the Sun to the ground, and the space behind you is dark. In this lesson you will see what light does when it meets different things: a screen, a mirror and a lens.
keynotes: Light travels in straight lines.
A shadow forms where your body blocks the straight path of the light.
The lesson looks at what light does at a screen, a mirror and a lens.

sections.title: A beam of light
sections.body:
Here is a small lamp that sends out a beam, and a screen that catches it. Press Simulate. Watch the beam leave the lamp and go straight across to the screen without bending.

Light is the fastest thing in the universe: about 300,000 kilometres every second. It could go around the Earth more than seven times in the time you blink once. Isn’t that amazing? Notice that the beam in the picture is a straight line.

figures.caption: Figure 1.1 — a lamp, a beam and a screen
figures.note: Press Simulate. Notice that the beam is a straight line.

keynotes: A beam of light goes straight from the lamp to the screen without bending.
Light travels about 300,000 kilometres every second, the fastest thing in the universe.
It could go around the Earth more than seven times in the time you blink once.

sections.title: Mirrors bounce light
sections.body:
What happens when light meets something shiny? It bounces! When light hits a smooth shiny surface such as a mirror, it bounces off. This is called reflection. The bounce follows a rule, the law of reflection: the angle the light comes in at equals the angle it goes out at.

That is why you can see yourself in a mirror: light from you reaches the mirror, bounces, and goes into your eyes. Press Simulate to watch the beam hit the mirror and bounce back. So if a ray makes an angle of 30° with the mirror’s straight-out line (the “normal”), at what angle does it leave? The same, 30°.

figures.caption: Figure 1.2 — light reflecting from a mirror
figures.note: Press Simulate. The beam hits the mirror and bounces back.

questions.prompt: A ray of light hits a flat mirror and makes an angle of 30° with the mirror's straight-out line (the "normal"). At what angle does it leave?

choices.text: 30° on the other side of the normal.

responses.title: That only happens if the light hits straight on.
responses.body: If it comes in along the normal, it goes straight back. This light comes in at an angle, so it bounces off at an angle.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The law of reflection says the angle in equals the angle out, measured from the normal. In at 30°, out at 30°, on the other side.

responses.title: The angle does not double.
responses.body: Reflection does not change the size of the angle, it only flips the direction. In at 30° means out at 30°.

keynotes: Light that hits a smooth shiny surface such as a mirror bounces off: reflection.
The law of reflection: the angle the light comes in at equals the angle it goes out at.
You see yourself in a mirror because light from you reaches the mirror, bounces and goes into your eyes.

sections.title: Lenses bend light
sections.body:
Glasses, cameras, magnifying glasses and your own eyes all use lenses. A lens is a piece of clear material shaped so that it bends light. A lens that is thick in the middle brings the beams together to one spot, called the focus.

How strongly it bends is described by its focal length, written f. A short focal length is a strong lens. A long one is a weak lens. Drag the slider and watch the spot move: a stronger lens (smaller f) brings the light to a point sooner. Try it, and see if you can predict where the spot will land.

figures.caption: Figure 1.3 — a lens bringing light to a focus
figures.note: Drag the slider to change the lens. A stronger lens (smaller f) brings the light to a point sooner.

keynotes: A lens is a piece of clear material shaped so that it bends light; one thick in the middle brings the beams together at the focus.
How strongly it bends is described by its focal length f: a short focal length is a strong lens and a long one is weak.
A stronger lens (smaller f) brings the light to a point sooner.

sections.title: Which lens is stronger?

questions.prompt: Lens A has a focal length of 50 mm. Lens B has a focal length of 200 mm. Which lens bends light more strongly?

choices.text: Lens A, because it brings the light to a focus sooner.
Lens B, because 200 is the bigger number.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A short focal length means the light is gathered to a point close to the lens, so the lens bends the light strongly. A magnifying glass is a short-focal-length lens.

responses.title: The bigger number is the weaker lens.
responses.body: The focal length is a distance, not a strength. A longer distance to the focus means the lens bends the light more gently.

responses.title: They are different.
responses.body: Same shape of idea, different strength. The one with the shorter focal length bends light more.

sections.body: Quick, guess first! Lens A has a focal length of 50 mm. Lens B has a focal length of 200 mm. Which lens bends light more strongly? Remember what you just learned about short and long focal lengths before you answer.
keynotes: Lens A has a focal length of 50 mm and lens B has 200 mm.
A shorter focal length means a stronger lens, so lens A bends light more strongly.

sections.title: How long is a light journey?
sections.body:
Let’s measure something huge. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us. How far away is the Sun? Light travels at 300,000 km/s. First, convert 8 minutes into seconds, because the speed is in km per second: 8 × 60 = 480 s. Distance is speed multiplied by time: d = v × t = 300 000 × 480 = 144 000 000 km.

That is about 144 million km. The true distance is about 150 million km. Our answer is close because “8 minutes” was rounded. Not bad for a sum you did at your desk!

worked.why: Convert 8 minutes into seconds, because the speed is in km per second.
Distance is speed multiplied by time.
That is about 144 million km. The true distance is about 150 million km. Our answer is close because "8 minutes" was rounded.

keynotes: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us, which is 8 × 60 = 480 s.
Distance is speed multiplied by time: 300 000 × 480 = 144 000 000 km.
The true distance is about 150 million km; our answer is close because 8 minutes was rounded.

sections.title: Try these

problems.prompt: Moonlight takes about 1.3 seconds to reach us. How far away is the Moon? (Light: 300,000 km/s.)
problems.answer: Distance = speed × time = 300,000 × 1.3 = 390,000 km. (The real distance is about 384,000 km.)

problems.prompt: Why can you not see around a corner, yet you can hear around a corner?
problems.answer: Light travels in straight lines, so a wall blocks it. Sound spreads out and bends around corners far more, so it reaches you.
